replying_to: Replying to Diffusion Models are Kelly Gamblers
display_title: Official Review of Submission5159 by Reviewer VRvv

summary.value: This paper introduces a number of conceptual connections between diffusion models, physics, and information theory. The main contribution is an analysis of how information about the label, Y, is dynamically injected into X during the diffusion dynamics. The machinery to calculate this comes from non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and results in an intuitive expression in terms of mutual information (which can be related to gambling via the Kelly criterion, motivating the title). The results are used to motivate discussion of qualitative properties of diffusion models like how CFG scale affects generation, the behavior of inter-pixel correlation during generation, and a variational interpretation of diffusion.

strengths.value:
The analysis of diffusion in terms of dynamical entropy production from Seifert and others was interesting. The notation and intuitions used in the molecular dynamics literature are quite different, so it was nice to see it adapted to this problem. I was curious how the choice of reverse protocol to define total entropy production is made, as Seifert gives several options. Perhaps this detail can be found in the reference provided. 

The TC(X) part was new to me, I have not seen a diffusion paper write or study this expression.

weaknesses.value:
The structure of the paper is unusual for ICLR. There are no empirical results presented in the main paper, these are all in the supplementary material. From this point of view, I'd consider this a "theory only" contribution. But as a theory paper it was unclear to me what the key result is that the paper was trying to build toward. 

# Key result / Contributions? 
I found the connections interesting, but it was hard me to pinpoint the specific contributions and whether each connection is superficial or not. 
 
-  Kelly criterion. An entire section (and the title) highlights the Kelly criterion, but this connection seemed incidental to me. I didn't see how it was used either in derivations or empirical results, besides adding an operational interpretation to mutual information. 

- Mutual information. 
One of the main contributions seems to be to give an alternate derivation of the mutual information expression from (Franzese, 2024) using the the stochastic thermodynamics ideas from (Seifert 2012) and (Premkumar 2025). 
But here again, the high level treatment leaves me wondering if anything significant is being stated. What is the difference between S (entropy using physics notation) and S_tot? Well, in Seifert S_tot is meant to include "total entropy production", which includes entropy that is added to the medium due to dissipation. Some particular assumptions are required to have a meaningful derivation for entropy added to the medium as we haven't explicitly modeled the medium in this context, and for these I had to go back to (Premkumar 2025) Appendix A. Regardless, we model total entropy production as entropy of the system plus the medium and we get results like Eq. 7 and 9 which are *regular entropy* plus some term, presumably related to dissipation in the medium. Then when we "derive" mutual information, the dissipation terms drop out and we get the standard expression S_X - S_X|Y. Did the detour to complexify the math by adding dissipation contribute in any way? I'm only a little familiar with Seifert 2012, but more than most people in this field. The explanation in the paper does not convey what is being done, nor justify why this machinery is necessary. I don't see how vague statements like the "network stores S_tot worth of information.." can be connected to the mathematical meaning of total entropy production. 
In the end, the final derivation of mutual information in C.1 doesn't use any ideas from Seifert anyway, that I can see. 



- Infinite tower. 
The reinterpretation in Eq. 24 doesn't really use or require quantum mechanics in any way.  The idea that each term in the sum/integral can be viewed as a separate "shallow" autoencoder is, I think, widely appreciated as no one trains a diffusion model by running the infinitely deep encoder, but rather by sampling an encoder that represents a term in the integral (Song & Ermon explicitly talk about this kind of shallow ensemble of autoencoders in their work). 


- Expressions like those in Eq. 22-23 are common in refs 1-3, and [5, Eq. 16]. The connection between MI and guidance is also explored in [1] below. 

# Related work 
The paper covers a lot of ideas relating diffusion to information theory, compression and variational methods, but the related work does not reflect existing work that has also explored these connections. 

- Information theory

[1] Information Theoretic Text-to-Image Alignment (ICLR 2025). This work analyzes the mutual information between text and images. They show that CFG scale increases mutual information, but they also include an analysis that shows that it decreases the overall visual quality, and propose an optimal trade-off. 

[2] Diffusion PID: Interpreting Diffusion via Partial Information Decomposition (NeurIPS 2024) 

[3] Information-Theoretic Proofs for Diffusion Sampling arXiv:2502.02305

[4] https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10084196. I saw and included this other one by Reeves, because it analyzes the mutual information in the Gaussian case specifically, which is what a lot of your empirical results in the appendix were based on. 

- Variational / autoencoder connections

[5] Variational Diffusion Models (NeurIPS 2021). I feel this is a kind of foundational paper for this connection.


- Compression 

[6] Progressive Compression with Universally Quantized Diffusion Models (ICLR 2025). The compression angle is discussed, there is lots of great work including this example.

questions.value:
My main question is for clarification of the intended contributions and which part of your arguments are novel compared to existing works.

Generally I'm very interested and excited about the physics connections presented, and hoping I can get clarification on the key results / contributions in the rebuttal stage.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission5159 by Reviewer VRvv

comment.value:
Thank you for the review, and specifically your physics questions. We address each of these below. Some of the concerns you raised were shared by other reviewers as well, especially relating to the key contributions and narrative structure. We have summarized our response to these shared critiques in the “Overall comments.”

Note: Lines, figures, and equation numbers refer to v1.

### Strengths

We appreciate the point you raise about the reverse protocol; we spent much time thinking about this. As mentioned in the paper, we end up taking the KL between the following two SDEs to obtain $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$:

$dX_t = -(b_{+} - \sigma^2 \nabla \log p) dt + \sigma dB_t,$

$dX_t = b_{+}\, dt + \sigma dB_t.$

The basic logic of doing so is explained in Premkumar (2025). Starting at $p_{\mathrm{eq}}$, the equilibrium state of the second equation, we will remain in that state if the system dynamics is governed by that equation. However, if we apply the first one we will drive the system away from $p_{\mathrm{eq}}$ and onto $p_{\mathrm{d}}$. The KL between the path measures generated by both processes is the total entropy. This is a version of the Jarzynski equality, specifically the form given in Eq. (10) of Vaikuntanathan and Jarzynski (2009). The Seifert reference was hinting at the fact that this is a fluctuation theorem.

Let us also address your comments about Seifert’s “entropy of the medium” argument. This notion is indeed problematic because it is not always clear what the medium is for some diffusive processes. A better physical picture is the one given in Appendix C.2 of Premkumar (2025), where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is defined in terms of *free energy*, $F[p] := E[p] - \beta^{-1} S[p]$, where $\beta := \sigma^2/2$. It is shown that $S_{\mathrm{tot}} = \beta (F[p_{\mathrm{d}}] - F[p_{\mathrm{eq}}]) \equiv -\beta \Delta F$. The $S[p]$ term is just the usual differential entropy of the distribution $p$. The term $E[p] := \mathbb{E}[-\int^x b_{+}]$ is the *energy* of the configuration $p$. Note that $\beta E[p]$ is the cross-entropy term, $\mathbb{E}[-\log p_{\mathrm{eq}}(x)] + \text{const.}$, since $\log p_{\mathrm{eq}}(x) \propto \int^x 2 b_{+} / \sigma^2$. This is also the piece Seifert interprets as "dissipation in the medium".

The free-energy formulation helps us connect to the standard picture in thermodynamics. A system tends to minimize its energy $E$, but it also wants to maximize its entropy $S$. Free energy is a combination of $E$ and $S$ such that the competing tendencies of energy minimization and entropy maximization become simply the minimization of $F$. That is, the minimum of $F$ is where $E$ and $S$ come to a compromise.

As an example, consider Fig. 7 in Premkumar (2025): $p_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is narrower than $p_{\mathrm{d}}$, so $S$ *decreases* from $s = 0 \to T$! This is only possible because a narrow $p_{\mathrm{eq}}$ implies a large confining drift term, so the system gains in energy minimization what it loses in entropy maximization, and therefore $\Delta F < 0$. In fact $\Delta F < 0$ for any diffusive process, which means $S_{\mathrm{tot}} > 0$. This is the Second Law.

A forward diffusion process that converts $p_{\mathrm{d}} \to p_{\mathrm{eq}}$ has traveled down the free-energy landscape to its minimum, with $\Delta F < 0$. Assuming some familiarity with statistical mechanics, or from Eq. (78) in Premkumar (2025), you can see that the probability that the system randomly fluctuates back to its original state $p_{\mathrm{d}}$ is  
$\propto e^{\beta N \Delta F} = e^{-N S_{\mathrm{tot}}}$.  Following Shannon, the information we need to “locate” $p_{\mathrm{d}}$ is the negative log of this probability. This is the amount of information the neural network must store/supply to generate $p_{\mathrm{d}}$ from $p_{\mathrm{eq}}$. Importantly, the information stored in the network is *not* $S[p_{\mathrm{eq}}] - S[p_{\mathrm{d}}]$; that would be negative for the example discussed above. This is the crux of Premkumar (2025).

We hope the above discussion illuminates the non-trivial nature of Eq. (10) in our paper,   $S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{X|Y} - S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{X} = I(X;Y)$.   In particular, the unconditional diffusion model stores $S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{X}$ worth of information, which includes $\beta \Delta E$. Crucially, the additional information stored in the conditional diffusion model is *on top of* $S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{X}$, and *not* $S(X)$.

Your question uncovers an important point that we have stressed in the new version: when we talk about how low $I(X;Y)$ can hurt the diffusion model’s adherence to the conditioning information, we mean that *$I(X;Y)$ is low compared to $S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{X}$, not compared to $S(X)$*. This distinction is crucial, and worth highlighting. Thank you!

comment.value:
We now turn our attention to the other points you raised.

### Weaknesses

1. *Organization:* We realize that the paper needs a tighter structure and sharper focus. We address this in the Overall comments.

2. *Relevance of Kelly:* See Overall comments.

3. *Mutual information:* Addressed above. We have added a brief review of Premkumar (2025) to the appendix to keep the paper self-contained.

4. *Infinite tower:* We tried to locate the picture of the ensemble of encoders in the Song and Ermon papers, but we could not find it. Can you pinpoint it for us? Also, the point of Sec. 6 was to show that diffusion models are not a *single* infinitely deep autoencoder as discussed in Huang et al. (2021), Tzen and Raginsky (2019), and C. Luo (2022). Rather, the autoencoders exist in parallel (see lines 437–445). This is *only* possible if the forward process has a Gaussian kernel, since that is what allows the more general integral in Eq. (45) to become Eq. (22). In turn, only the latter can be exactly matched with the Fermi Golden Rule; if the process were not Gaussian, higher terms in the Dyson-series expansion would come into play and the decomposition in (24) would no longer describe the diffusion model (see Sakurai). This is also why Gaussian kernels are so important in the “simulation-free” training of diffusion models. We have moved Sec. 6 to the appendix to integrate it more tightly with the derivations in App. B and to simplify the main story without distractions.

[1] Tzen, B. and Raginsky, M., "Neural Stochastic Differential Equations: Deep Latent Gaussian Models in the Diffusion Limit", arXiv:1905.09883, 2019.

[2] C. Luo, "Understanding Diffusion Models: A Unified Perspective", August 2022.

### Relevant literature

Thank you for these references. Many of these are new to us and did not appear in our initial literature search. We have cited them in the updated manuscript. We had a quick look at them.

[1] *Information Theoretic Text-to-Image Alignment (ICLR 2025):* While this paper does discuss how they can lower the CFG scale and still maintain good alignment through their fine-tuning approach, we could not find a deeper analysis of how CFG affects the mutual information directly. Our Sec. 4 does this.

[2] *Diffusion PID:* Much of the methodology in this paper is similar to the papers by Kong et al. We have addressed the relation between our work and theirs in the rebuttal to fA2j (see Weaknesses / Grounding in existing literature). As explained there, our formulas are more general than those in Kong et al.

[3] *Information-Theoretic Proofs for Diffusion Sampling:* This is a really nice paper, thank you! The I-MMSE relation they discuss is the same one mentioned above, from Kong et al.

[4] *Reeves 2:* This paper does use the $Y = AX + \varepsilon$ model from our experiments. We have cited it.

[5] *Variational Diffusion Models:* Cited in the new version.

[6] *Progressive Compression with Universally Quantized Diffusion Models:* The core message of this paper expands on the Huffman-coding intuition we allude to in line 402. More broadly, the idea of a codec that can produce a progressive stream of bits and decode at increasing fidelity levels fits nicely with the picture we were trying to construct with the “infinite tower.” This reference has been incorporated into that discussion.

### Questions

We have re-organized the paper to highlight the core message more clearly. See also Overall comments. This should make the novel contributions much more apparent.

We are heartened by your enthusiasm for the physics/information-theory perspective. We hope the changes we made to the paper allay your concerns. If so, we would be much obliged if you could revise your score accordingly. Thank you again for the many interesting questions and suggestions for improvement. It was delightful to dig into the nuances of stochastic thermodynamics in this discussion.

comment.value:
First, I want to say that I appreciate that you are bringing some unconventional points of view to this problem. That can be challenging for readers, but I'm happy that you are trying to bridge the gap and hope you aren't too put off by some of the negative reactions. 

I'm most of the way through the significantly revised version and I really like the new version much better. 
- I found the introduction of entropy production in Sec. 3 much clearer and more intuitive. I'm beginning to appreciate the value of this quantity, compared to entropy. Emphasizing the KL with the equilibrium distribution, and writing out and describing p_eq was helpful. Because entropy production is non-negative and has an operational meaning, I can start to see how you can make the statements about how much information comes from different aspects (internal correlations, versus label, e.g.), in a way which doesn't really make sense when you talk about differential entropy, as you now point out.  
- I'm still not totally sold on the value of the Kelly angle, but I appreciate that you incorporate this perspective more consistently. I agree it is a novel and worthwhile way to look at generative models.  And the Kelly perspective is tied to bets regarding the concrete generative dynamics here, so I the link is a bit more clear to me now. 
- I'll try to read through your rebuttal points on the "tower of autoencoders" and see if I misunderstood this, but I think the paper reads much better with this moved from the main text.

comment.value:
Thank you for the words of encouragement.  Honestly, we debated whether it was even worthwhile to engage in rebuttal since some of the scores seemed unsalvageable. But we stand firm on the science, and we are glad that it comes through more emphatically now.

Regarding your points,

1. *Entropy production:* This is great! We're relieved the core message about 'how much information comes from different aspects (internal correlations, versus label, e.g.)' is more evident now.

2. *Kelly:* To be fully transparent, the "aha" moment for this paper came to us when we were reading Kelly's paper, so the title is partly an homage. More concretely, Kelly was trying to give meaning to MI outside of Shannon's coding theorems. His message was that MI measures correlations and correlations give you an edge in betting games. It is absolutely possible to make the points in this paper without invoking Kelly, but the connection would be right there.

3. *Images experiments:* Till reviewer mLfw pointed it out to us, we thought we were still restricted to 9 pages. We'd be happy to include more detail for the image experiments in the main text if it is not sufficiently clear. In simple terms, we're using the DAE to check how much label specific information is carried in different intervals of the forward diffusion process.

We look forward to hearing your thoughts.

display_title: Official Review of Submission5159 by Reviewer 9PhK

summary.value: Conditional diffusion models need to generate high-quality images consistent with a given prompt or label. This is not necessarily computationally easy, since the word "dog" is associated with an extremely large number of complex images, and is hence not that informative about individual pixel colors and intensities. The authors claim that diffusion models learn a 'rational' strategy which is analogous to satisfying the Kelly criterion in betting games.

strengths.value:
The writing is grammatical and stylish, and there are few figures (one in the main text, more in SI) but they are nice-looking. The paper appears to be quite original and the authors demonstrate knowledge of a wide range of fields. 

The insight that an information-theoretic perspective can help us understand why diffusion models work well, and in particular why classifier-free guidance works well, is interesting.

weaknesses.value:
This paper is really frustrating. While the language is nice and the ideas sound original, the more I go over its various points, the more I find them unclear and lacking in support. Overall, I am left with an impression that this paper is more poetry than substance. 

**What precisely is being claimed?** The first issue is that it is not exactly clear in many cases what the claims of the paper are. Almost all of the math is known, and there are almost no experiments (in the main text, at least; I did not read the SI in detail). As far as I can tell, the claims are mostly of an 'interpretive' nature: this is potentially an interesting way to *think* about diffusion models. While new ways of thinking can be intrinsically interesting, it isn't clear to me what the consequences or predictions of this are.

I'm still confused about the Kelly gambler analogy, and am more confused the more I think about it. For example, what does it mean to "bet" or "invest" here? It seems like the meat of the analogy is that both betting and sample generation involve mutual information (MI) and conditional MI. But I'm not sure what to make of it beyond that. If the authors claim that diffusion models are implicitly solving an optimal control problem (say, a problem where one has to choose how to invest bits of information at different times during sample generation, or something like that), they should spell out that problem and show how diffusion models solve it optimally compared to other possible strategies. 

Another subtle issue with the titular claim of the paper is that a lot of the math actually studies "entropy-matching models" introduced by a paper from earlier this year (see line 181); these are different from what the authors call "score-matching models", which are what people normally think of as "diffusion models". **This is a really big deal!** It feels like a sleight of hand; it feels like the authors liked the Kelly gambler analogy, and modified diffusion models until it became true-ish.

**Support for claims.** As I said above, I can't find new math results or nontrivial experiments. Also, a lot of the math applies to "entropy-matching models" rather than diffusion models proper. The paper makes a lot of claims about how diffusion models behave, and why they work, and so on. Frankly, the number of such claims per page is dizzying. 

It's possible that they are all interesting and true. I am definitely open to this possibility. But the authors should really focus on a few of them (especially the titular claim) and show that they really are true. Moreover, the truth of these claims ideally has some interesting consequence or yields interesting predictions.

A given claim should have some combination of math, experiments, and citations to support it. Interesting claims which are 'intuitively' or probably true should be removed and supported in future work.

**Gibberish.** Some of the claims made are slightly unhinged. Consider especially Section 6, the last section: in it, the authors claim that (i) "a diffusion model is an infinite tower of variational autoencoders" and that (ii) a decomposition of the log-likelihood relevant to diffusion models resembles Fermi's golden rule from quantum mechanics. 

I'm not sure what to make of these claims. I am not excited to say this; I've used the Sakurai quantum mechanics textbook the authors cite. What is the substance? What is being said about how diffusion models work? What are the new predictions/consequences? Like the Kelly gambler analogy, it seems like the authors are squinting and seeing a vague relationship, but it is not clear if the relationship is useful or interesting. Moreover, the claims of the last section appear to not relate to the Kelly gambler claims much. My impression is that the authors have packed a lot of 'this might be kind of cool' material into a loosely organized package.

**Overall assessment.** I value the authors' attempt to leverage work from information theory and physics to better understand diffusion models. I really do value theoretical insight of this kind. But I think significant restructuring, new evidence, and tamping down of claims would be necessary to make this paper coherent.

questions.value:
My most important questions are these:

1. What new consequences/predictions does the Kelly gambler view yield? Also, can you explain it better? What does it mean for a diffusion model to "bet" or "invest"? Is there some sort of way to formalize the betting problem and show trained diffusion models solve it well?

2. Can the authors clarify which of their claims (e.g., the Kelly gambler one) apply just to entropy-matching models, versus both entropy-matching models and more conventional diffusion models? This wasn't clear to me.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission5159 by Reviewer 9PhK

comment.value:
Thank you for your review. Before we address your points, we want to make a comment about your review itself. While we value your critique, it is possible to avoid phrases like “this paper is more poetry than substance,” “the number of such claims per page is dizzying,” “gibberish,” and “claims made are unhinged.” We are all trying our best to do good science, but sometimes the outcomes are imperfect. We hope that you are open to our revisions. We will address your comments and questions in good faith.

Note: Lines, figures, and equation numbers refer to v1.

### Weaknesses

1. *Narrative focus:* We admit that the paper has some structural issues, as other reviewers also noted. We have updated the paper to fix this, as explained in the Overall comments. The substance of the paper should come through more clearly now.

2. *“New” math:* The paper is not about introducing new math, but about finding connections in the existing math. For instance, in Sec. 3 we relate the arguments from Premkumar (2025) to Kelly (1956). In Sec. 4 we relate CFG to the core result of Franzese et al. (2023). We show the connection between neural entropy and total correlation in Eq. (11), and use all of these to explain why diffusion models often forget their conditioning. These points are emphasized more sharply in the new version.

3. *Experiments:* The paper contains at least five different experiments, with some of them having sub-experiments within them. Yes, these are in the appendix, but we have mentioned them multiple times in the main text (see lines 220, 261, 296, and 429). We understand that reviewers are not required to read the SI, and we take responsibility for not summarizing the experiments in the main text in v1. But the paper *does* have several experiments to back up the central claims; they are not merely intuition or “poetry.”

4. *Entropy matching:* The substitution $s_{\theta} = \nabla \log p_{\mathrm{eq}}^{(t)} + e_{\theta}$ turns a score-matching model into an entropy-matching model, as evident from Eq. (6). For a VP process it is simply $s_{\theta} = -x + e_{\theta}$. *Every insight in our paper carries through if you eliminate $e_{\theta}$ in favor of $s_{\theta}$ using this formula.*

   The connection between $s_{\theta}$ and $e_{\theta}$ is discussed in Premkumar (2025) and in line 905 of our paper. We make this more explicit in the updated version. We stress that the parameterization of the reverse drift, $-b_{+} + \sigma^2 s_{\theta}$ vs. $b_{+} + \sigma^2 e_{\theta}$, or anything in between, is purely a matter of choice (see line 182). We take your point that score matching was popularized in early diffusion-model literature, but it does *not* mean that “diffusion models = score matching.” In fact, the entropy-matching objective is identical to the flow-matching loss for diffusion from Y. Lipman et al. (2022).

   The point of using entropy matching is to guarantee that the neural network stores **only** $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ worth of information and nothing more. Score-matching models store an additional amount of information to counteract the $-x$ drift. Therefore, entropy-matching models are more transparent to analyze. Given these points, the concerns about EM vs. SM are not as severe as stated.

5. *Connection to Kelly criterion:* Kelly tells us that our win rate is optimal if we bet according to the true distribution of outcomes. Thus, Kelly gambling is fundamentally a problem in probabilistic modeling. See Overall comments. We have emphasized the connection to Kelly in v2.

6. *Support for claims:* These points have been addressed above. The paper does contain math and experiments to back up the claims. These have been integrated more tightly in the new version. Some new experiments have been added as well.

comment.value:
7. *“Gibberish”:* Reviewers mLfw and VRvv remarked that claim (i)—“a diffusion model is an infinite tower of variational autoencoders”—was more or less obvious, while it was “unhinged” in your view. This left us somewhat confused. To their point, there are other works which decompose diffusion models into infinite VAEs, but we point out that there are subtleties not captured in those papers (see rebuttal to Weakness 4 in VRvv’s review, lines 436–445). These subtleties follow from drawing a connection to the Fermi Golden Rule.

   Since you indicated familiarity with Sakurai, you will appreciate the following point: the Golden Rule comes from the linear term in the Dyson-series expansion in perturbation theory. Yet, Eq. (23)/(24) in our paper is exact. This is because Eq. (22) is a special case of the more general expression for log density, Eq. (45), namely the case of a Gaussian perturbation, $\tilde{x}_s = \mu(s)\, x + \Sigma(s)\, \varepsilon$, which is *also linear*. In other words, *only* Gaussian channels admit the infinite-VAE interpretation.

   The original intent of this section was to connect the singular behavior of neural entropy to the iterative nature in which diffusion models inject information. But we see that this was not adequately emphasized in the main text of v1, so Sec. 6 felt out of place. We have therefore moved Sec. 6 to the appendix, which also brings it closer to the derivations in App. B. We have also emphasized the above point about Gaussian kernels. This section will no longer distract from the main story.

8. *Overall assessment:* We appreciate your open-mindedness to the possibility that the claims are true. We have edited the paper to streamline the flow and bring the claims and evidence closer together.

[1] Kong, Xianghao, Rob Brekelmans, and Greg Ver Steeg. “Information-theoretic diffusion.” arXiv:2302.03792 (2023).

### Questions

1. See Relevance to Kelly as well as the Main messages in the Overall comments.
2. See *Entropy Matching* in the Weaknesses above.

We appreciate your perspective, and we have made changes to reflect your comments. We urge you to reconsider your rating in light of these changes. Please let us know if you have further questions or comments.

display_title: Official Review of Submission5159 by Reviewer mLfw

summary.value: The authors analyze diffusion models through the lens of entropy and mutual information, leading to analysis of the effect of conditioning on labels via guidance or latent variables in diffusion autoencoders.   The entropy-matching perspective draws connections with stochastic thermodynamics and lends itself readily to analysis of information-theoretic quantities.

strengths.value:
I am very much in favor of information theoretic perspectives on generative models such as VAEs or diffusion models.   The entropy matching perspective in the paper lends itself nicely to reasoning about information theoretic quantities.   

I like the empirical investigation of the mutual information of CFG-guided models with $w > 1$ in App. Fig 4.   Motivated by lines 263-272, this involves fitting a further conditional diffusion model to samples generated with CFG and estimating MI using Eq 13-14.  

My opinion of the paper improved dramatically upon reading through the Appendix, where intuitively reasonable qualitative statements in the paper were supported by evidence.   As discussed in Weaknesses below, I think this analysis should be more tightly integrated into the main text to further strengthen the paper.


The paper covers a wide range of topics related to information theoretic quantities in diffusion models, although take-home messages should be more tightly packaged (see below).   I imagine the number of topics could be reduced to provide a more focused and streamlined paper.

weaknesses.value:
I am left struggling to isolate the main contribution of the paper.    
- Based on my reading of the paper and comments below, I believe the authors have material that *might* be used to argue that
    - (i) analysis of the properties of mutual information in diffusion models with label vs. latent variable conditioning 
    - leads to (ii) recommendations on how to provide better conditioning mechanism for diffusion models.   

However, the current submission seems to lack the structured arguments to lead to any such recommendations.

*Grounding Conclusions in Empirical Evidence*

The paper is strongest when providing empirical evidence to link statements about MI and statements about diffusion models. Having established these links, ideally we would obtain insight into how to best condition our diffusion models in scenarios of interest.
*Unfortunately, most empirical evidence for main text statements is relegated to the Appendix.*

For example:
- In Lines 274-296, the point that "perceptual details contribute the more entropy than labels" is succinctly supported by App Fig 8 (the unconditional model might also be interesting to show alongside to strengthen the claim).  This should be in the main text.
    - L 285-286 "This is why diffusion models often stray from the conditioning signal during generation:  the mutual information between images and labels is intrinsically low" could be supported by calculating MI for a standard conditional vs. unconditional model (alongside the below).
- The saturation of CFG in App Fig 4 seems interesting to analyze and discuss in detail within this context (on images?).  For example, this could replace and/or strengthen Line 353-354 "However, CFG does have a fundamental limitation:  if the underlying dependence between X and Y is weak, amplification of the signal can only go so far."
- This would seem to provide principled motivation for an argument in favor of conditioning with learned autoencoder representations $Z$.

Thank you for your detailed review and many valuable suggestions. We appreciate the fact that your review seems to be the most thorough out of the four. We have incorporated many of your suggestions into the new version.

Note: Lines, figures, and equation numbers refer to v1.

### Strengths

Thank you for having a look at the appendix. Your point about sharpening the core messages is well-taken (see below).

### Weaknesses

1. *Narrative focus:* The main contribution is a new theoretical perspective, which we have summarized in the Overall comment. This is highlighted more emphatically in the updated version.

2. *Empirical evidence:* We restructured the paper to move the old Sec. 5 and 6 to the appendix, and used this space to present a shortened version of the empirical results in the main text. We have kept Fig. 8 in the appendix because we ran out of space, but the core message about perceptual details overwhelming the information budget is now front and center in v2. In addition, we have added both conditional and unconditional entropies for image models in that figure, as you suggested. The MI values are reported in the caption, because they are three orders of magnitude smaller than the neural entropy.

3. *CFG:* It appears you are asking for a direct comparison of $I(X;Y)_{\mathrm{CFG}}$ with $I(X;Z)$. This is a great suggestion. However, as part of simplifying the narrative in v2 we have removed any recommendations about CFG vs. latent conditioning from the main paper. There is a story to be told here, but we think it would be better conveyed in a separate paper.

4. *Text-prompts:* One of the key takeaways from the new version is that MI between the labels and images is more or less orthogonal to the singular behavior of $\mathrm{TC}(X)$ (or $S_{\mathrm{tot}}^{X}$). We expect this to still be true for text-prompts, due to the limited “channel capacity” of the prompts in relation to the $\mathrm{TC}(X)$ of the images. The dimension-wise MI results in your [3,4] are nice; we found similar plots in [1]. We note that $\mathrm{TC}(X)$ captures the correlation between the pixels in a more collective manner, but it is harder to visualize.

5. *DAE / Information Bottleneck:* $\gamma$ controls the trade-off between compression and distortion. The discussion in lines 338–348 is a thought experiment, where we effectively adjust the *width* of the bottleneck to regulate how much the diffusion decoder commits to the training samples. $\gamma$ is assumed to be fixed here. In principle, a similar effect also arises if we adjust the strength of $\gamma$: smaller $\gamma$ widens the bottleneck and larger $\gamma$ tightens it. However, the bottleneck is also strongly influenced by the dimensionality of $Z$: lower $D_Z$ limits $I(X;Z)$. This is why, for the purposes of the thought experiment, we chose to play around with $D_Z$ rather than $\gamma$.

   Our information bottleneck is $X \to Z \to X$. This was sufficient for the context in which we used the IB, namely the $(Z_{\mathrm{per}}, Z_{\mathrm{sem}})$ experiments where we *did not want the latents to know about the classes other than through $X$*. The point of the latter experiments was to demonstrate that the information in $s \in (0,\tau)$ is not correlated with the class label. That said, we did experiment with having a $Z \to Y$ decoder to apply pressure on $Z$. Our initial experiments did not show much improvement in clustering for a DAE, so this line of inquiry was abandoned.

6. *Additional questions/comments:*

   a. *Relevance of Kelly:* See Main messages 1 and 2, and the “Relevance to Kelly” section in the Overall comment. Essentially, we are saying that the core problem in gambling and generative modeling is the same: we want to model a probability distribution as faithfully as possible. In addition, we point out that Kelly’s original paper “A New Interpretation of Information Rate” was *about* mutual information: he was trying to give it meaning outside the context of Shannon’s coding theorems. Kelly’s key message is that MI measures correlations. Our paper explores how diffusion models absorb correlations worth $\mathrm{TC}(X)$ and $I(X;Y)$.

   We have refined Sec. 2 to clarify the exposition and emphasize the connection between betting and generative modeling.

   b. *Continuous MI:* The discussion in lines 289–292 is meant to show that (1) continuous MI can be infinite, and (2) the same pathology appears in $\mathrm{TC}(\vec{X})$ since MI and $\mathrm{TC}$ have the same KL-divergence structure. We understand how reusing the symbol $Y$ may cause confusion here; we have modified the discussion to be about $I(X_1; X_2)$ so it connects to the total correlation *between* the components of $\vec{X}$ more seamlessly.

   c. *Typos:* $L_{DEM}$ and the typos in $Z_{\mathrm{sem}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{per}}$ are fixed. Some more explanation of these latents has been added in the main text.

[1] Harrigan, C., “Estimation of Mutual Information for Image Classification”, March 2019.

### Questions

1. *Fermi Golden Rule:* Eqs. (21)–(23) are not new, as you noted. The discussion in Sec. 6 is about the *interpretation* of these equations. Specifically, lines 378–403 note that the integral in (23) has a “sum over intermediate states” or “sum over histories” structure that is ubiquitous in quantum mechanics. This discussion is what helps us eventually arrive at Eq. (24). The innermost integrand in (24) is an information-bottleneck / autoencoder $X \to \tilde{X}_s \to X'$. The integral over time shows that the diffusion model factorizes into an infinite number of such bottlenecks, each at a given time/noise scale $s$. Lines 436–445 articulate how this picture differs from the more popular view of diffusion models as infinitely deep VAEs. We have moved this section to the appendix to make room in the main text and reduce distractions from the streamlined story.

2. *Equilibrium state:* Neural entropy is the amount of information the diffusion model applies to push the system from $p_{\mathrm{eq}}^{(t)}$. The point of defining neural entropy with respect to this measure (entropy-matching) is that it guarantees that the neural network stores *only* $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ worth of information. Our $p_{\mathrm{eq}}$ can be any well-defined distribution. The discussion in Kong et al. (2023) is a special case of our Eq. (4), when $\nabla \log p_{\mathrm{eq}} \propto -x$. The Jarzynski and Seifert references cited there pre-date it by quite a lot. We cite the reference you mentioned nonetheless. See also the rebuttal to Weakness 1 in fA2j’s review.

We hope that we have addressed your concerns to your satisfaction. If so, we implore you to reconsider your rating to reflect the new manuscript. In any case, we are grateful for your meticulous and thoughtful review, which has undoubtedly improved the paper in many ways.

summary.value: This paper presents a novel theoretical perspective linking diffusion models to the Kelly criterion from information theory. The core idea is that when a diffusion model generates a sample $X$ conditioned on some variable $Y$, it behaves like a Kelly gambler who bets optimally using side information to maximize long-term growth, in this case, maximizing mutual information. Overall, the paper’s framing is creative but lacks sufficient novelty, theoretical rigor, and empirical evidence to substantiate its claims. Strengthening literature grounding, adding original experiments, and clarifying contributions would greatly improve it.

strengths.value: The main strength of this paper lies in its unifying interdisciplinary theoretical insight: it elegantly bridges generative diffusion modeling, information theory, and optimal decision-making by showing that conditional diffusion models act like Kelly gamblers. This framing clarifies how diffusion models implicitly manage information between data and conditions, recasting classifier-free guidance as an information amplification mechanism that increases mutual information between the generated sample and its condition.

weaknesses.value:
1. While the paper introduces an appealing new connecting between diffusion models and the Kelly criterion, the underlying idea of linking information theory and generative modeling is not new. Prior works such as Kong et al. [1,2] on Information-Theoretic Diffusion, Franzese et al., [3] and Yu et al. [4] have already analyzed diffusion models through a mutual information lens, addressing information transport, entropy flow, and guidance mechanisms. Moreover, several papers have used diffusion models explicitly for mutual information estimation. The current work neither cites nor situates itself clearly within this body of literature.

2. Many concepts (e.g., Entropy Matching [5], DAE [6], Neural Entropy [5]) are reformulations of existing ideas. The new terms like Kelly Criterion and Infinite Tower are briefly introduced but not developed into rigorous theory or practical insight.

3. Most experiments in the appendix appear reused from Neural Entropy [5] with little new validation of the proposed Kelly-gambler framework. 

4. The paper’s interdisciplinary framing mixes information theory, generative modeling, and physics in a dense, sometimes confusing way. Simplifying terminology and focusing on the central argument would improve readability. 


[1] Kong, Xianghao, Rob Brekelmans, and Greg Ver Steeg. "Information-theoretic diffusion." arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.03792 (2023).

[2] Kong, Xianghao, et al. "Interpretable diffusion via information decomposition." arXiv preprint arXiv:2310.07972 (2023).

[3] Franzese, Giulio, Mustapha Bounoua, and Pietro Michiardi. "MINDE: Mutual information neural diffusion estimation." arXiv preprint arXiv:2310.09031 (2023).

[4] Yu, Longxuan, et al. "MMG: Mutual Information Estimation via the MMSE Gap in Diffusion." arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.20609 (2025).

[5] Premkumar, Akhil. "Neural entropy." arXiv preprint arXiv:2409.03817 (2024).

[6] Preechakul, Konpat, et al. "Diffusion autoencoders: Toward a meaningful and decodable representation." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2022.

Thank you for your time and effort in reviewing our paper. Many of the shared concerns from the reviews, about the core message and narrative framing, are addressed in the "Overall comments". We will address your specific concerns below, focusing on your complaints about "sufficient novelty, theoretical rigor, and empirical evidence to substantiate its claims."

On theoretical rigor, we have supplied detailed proofs for most claims in the main text in App. B and C, with a completely novel proof based on stochastic control for the MINDE formula, Eq. (13). This is the main result in the paper by Franzese et al. (2024). Other theoretic results, especially from Premkumar (2025) have simply been cited, and we do not prove them again here.

There are at least five different experiments in the paper, as enumerated at the beginning of App. D. We take full responsibility for not summarizing these experiments in the main text, which is an issue multiple reviewers brought up. It has been rectified in the new version. We have also added new set of experiments simulating the manifold structure of $X$. The novelty of these experiments is addressed below.

Note: Lines and equation numbers refer to v1.

### Weaknesses

1. *Grounding in existing literature:* We do not claim that we are the first to link information theory and generative modeling. In fact, many of the papers we borrow from already make such connections. Our insights come from stochastic thermodynamics, which pre-date several of the references you mentioned. For instance, Eq. (4) in our paper is just a version of the Jarzynski relation, which has been known since the 90s. We cite papers by Vaikuntanathan and Jarzynski (2009), Seifert (2012), and later Ge and Jiang (2008) and Huang et al. (2021) as references for Eq. (4). The discussion in Sec. 3 of Kong et al. (2023), titled "Diffusion as thermodynamic integration", is a *specific case* of our Eq. (37) when $\nabla \log p_{\mathrm{eq}} \propto -x$. This corresponds to the Gaussian channel, as explained around Eqs. (43) and (44) in our paper. These formulas appear in the other references too. In particular Eq. (10) in our paper, $S^{X|Y}_{tot} - S^{X}_{tot} = I(X;Y)$, is *more general* than Eq. (8) of Yu et al. or Eq. (4) in Kong et al. (2023), since our formula is valid for any well-defined $p_{\mathrm{eq}}$ and not just the Gaussian case. Similarly, the Franzese formula for $I(X;Y)$, our Eq. (13), generalizes Eq. (5) of Kong et al. (2023) beyond the Gaussian case. That said, we have added new citations for [1, 2, 4] from your list in the v2.

2. *Synthesis:* The aforementioned papers, as well as Franzese, discuss calculation of MI using diffusion models, but they do not talk about the information **stored** in the neural network. Premkumar (2024) does this, but there is hardly any mention of mutual information. Our work synthesizes these two ideas and connects $\mathrm{TC}(X)$ and $I(X;Y)$ with the information *stored* in the neural network. We are not trying to develop a new method to compute MI; we are interested in understanding how diffusion models capture correlations and how this affects their ability to generate samples/place bets. See Overall comments / Main messages.

3. *Experiments:* We have performed experiments in the style of Premkumar (2024), yes, but there are several experiments, those with CFG and with the DAE, which go well beyond anything in that paper. See Figs. 1, 4, 7, 9, 10. These are summarized better in the new version. We have also added a new set of experiments with the $Y = AX + \varepsilon$ model where $X$ is flattened to a low-rank distribution to simulate image manifolds.

4. *Narrative focus:* Your point about narrative focus is echoed by the other reviewers as well. We hear you and have re-organized the paper to reflect the feedback.

Thank you once again for your review. We hope that the new version allays your concerns, and that you would consider updating the score accordingly. We welcome follow-up discussions and questions.

We are grateful to the reviewers for their time and effort, and for the insightful comments and questions. We admit that we tried to squeeze a large number of ideas into one paper, and it is clearly poorer for it, based on the collective feedback. A recurring critique was that the section with experiments was relegated to the appendix. We did so because we did not want to break it up to squeeze into the main text. But we see that this approach forces the reader to flip back and forth between the main and appendix, and the reviewers who did not do so found our arguments vacuous. These choices reflect our limited experience writing for ML conferences. However, we believe that there are meaningful and novel insights in the paper, which we have surfaced more clearly in the new version. Most, if not all, of your concerns are addressed in this updated manuscript.

We have moved Sec. 5 on "DAE" and Sec. 6 on "The Infinite Tower" to the appendix, and used the space to summarize the empirical results and refocus the narrative. Specifically, we noticed that the manifold story went largely unnoticed, for which we take full responsibility. This is now part of the main text. We have added new experiments and appendices, as suggested by reviewers. We reiterate the main story below, and address some of the shared criticism. More individualized rebuttals are given as replies to the respective reviewers.

## Relevance to Kelly

Reviewers have felt a disconnect between the title of the paper and its contents. We would like to point out that *Kelly gambling is fundamentally a problem of probabilistic modeling: Kelly tells us that capital must be allocated proportional to the probability of outcomes, so the winnings depend on how accurately one's internal model captures the true distribution of said outcomes* (see also Theorem 6.1.2 in Cover and Thomas: "Proportional gambling is log-optimal"). This is also the core problem of generative modeling. While this point was obvious to us, it was clearly not conveyed properly in v1. We have emphasized it in the new version.

A signal that is correlated with the game's outcomes lets us focus our bets on a narrower range of high-probability outcomes. For example, it could be past performance, or some concurrent event that is related to the game. Our returns depend on how well they correlate with the outcome, which is measured by mutual information. Diffusion models are doing the same thing: the signal is the training data and the diffusion model concentrates the probability mass from the initial Gaussian according to this data. The connection to betting manifests in two ways:

1. An unconditional diffusion model trained on samples of $X$ learns the internal correlations between the components of $X$. This is captured by $\mathrm{TC}(X)$, which is a multivariate version of mutual information. In other words, the diffusion model makes a *joint bet* on all $x_k$ components when it generates a new sample of $X$.

2. Conditional diffusion models trained on samples of $(X,Y)$ store an additional $I(X;Y)$ information to relate $X$ with $Y$ (e.g., images and labels). The signal $Y$ allows further narrowing of the probability mass from $p(x)$ to $p(x \mid y)$.

## Main messages

We summarize and clarify the core messages of the paper below. The introduction has been rewritten to emphasize these points from the start.

1. Kelly betting is a problem of modeling the distribution of a game's outcomes. Side information allows us to tighten our internal probabilistic model, allowing us to make more informed bets than the other player (dealer).

2. Diffusion models are also probabilistic models. In training a diffusion model we are implicitly trying to make it Kelly-optimal. That is, we are trying to make it absorb $S_{\mathrm{tot}}^X$ (which contains $\mathrm{TC}(X)$) and an additional $I(X;Y)$, because that is how much information it needs to model $p(x)$ and $p(x \mid y)$ accurately.

3. In practical diffusion models, $I(X;Y)$ is much smaller than $S_{\mathrm{tot}}^X$ (three orders of magnitude in the image case). This is because $S_{\mathrm{tot}}^X$ measures the effort required to squeeze the initial Gaussian ball into the target distribution, which usually lives on a low-dimensional manifold. $\mathrm{TC}(X)$ is the singular part of $S_{\mathrm{tot}}^X$.

4. Despite this, diffusion models can still produce reasonable estimates of $I(X;Y)$, because *the information applied to locate the $X$ manifold is largely irrelevant to correlating $X$ and $Y$*. We prove this with a new set of experiments with the joint Gaussian, and highlight experiments with the DAE on images. It also explains why classifier-free guidance is effective.

comment.value:
Dear AC/members of the decision committee,

We are saddened to see the decision to stick with the initial scores, though we understand why such a measure is needed to protect the integrity of the review process. We make one final, respectful appeal to consider our paper for inclusion in ICLR 2025.

Our initial reviews were lukewarm largely because our narrative structure was not as clear as it should have been. This weakened the presentation of our main ideas and led to understandable confusion about our core message. As first-time ICLR authors, we misjudged the expectations for ML conference writing, and we take full responsibility for that. At the same time, we remain confident in the novelty and scientific value of the underlying contributions.

We worked tirelessly after the initial reviews to produce a much more focused version of the paper in just **8 days**. A simple pdfdiff between the initial submission and the current version will make the extent our revisions immediately apparent. We also provided highly detailed, point-by-point responses to each reviewer comment, as documented in the rebuttal. Of the reviewers who replied before the discussion was frozen, one (VRvv) explicitly noted that the revised version was “much better.”

We are confident that, had things gone smoothly, and with full reviewer engagement, we could have moved the scores to a much more favorable range. Unfortunately, we no longer have the ability to demonstrate this through the usual channels. We sincerely hope that our efforts and the scientific merit of our work will still be given full and fair consideration.

Thank you.

summary.value:
This paper proposes a reinterpretation of diffusion models using entropy production, total correlation, and a Kelly-gambling analogy. While the perspective is intellectually interesting, the core contribution remains largely interpretive rather than substantive. The paper mainly reframes known results in new language without yielding clear, tractably testable predictions or algorithmic consequences.

When conditioning is ignored, the main claim reduces to the observation that diffusion models “inject the information needed to reconstruct the data,” which is close to tautological. The emphasis on neural entropy and total correlation is conceptually appealing, but these quantities are computationally intractable for real models, so it remains unclear how the framework could be operationalized or validated beyond toy settings.

reviewer_concerns.value: The rebuttal improved the clarity of the narrative and partly addressed concerns about structure, especially by moving speculative material to the appendix and emphasizing entropy production more clearly. It also added missing citations and somewhat clarified the relation between entropy-matching and standard score-based models. However, major concerns remain unresolved: the work still lacks a precise statement of what is genuinely new, the Kelly analogy remains largely rhetorical, and the key information-theoretic quantities are not computable in realistic settings, so the claims cannot be experimentally validated. The paper continues to function primarily as an interpretive reframing rather than delivering concrete, testable contributions.

reviewer_scores.value: I think they would remain unchanged.
